lesson.title: No DHCP Required: How a Device Addresses Itself with SLAAC
lesson.summary: IPv6's stateless address autoconfiguration, SLAAC, lets a device build its own valid, routable address by combining a network prefix learned from a router advertisement with an interface identifier it generates itself, without ever contacting a DHCP server.
lesson.body:
IPv4 devices almost always get their address from a DHCP server, a stateful process where a central server hands out and tracks address leases. IPv6 was designed to make address assignment work without that dependency whenever possible, through a mechanism called Stateless Address Autoconfiguration, universally abbreviated SLAAC. The word stateless is the key distinction: no server anywhere needs to track which address it handed to which device, because the device computes its own address using information it gathers locally and from the network, relying on the address format concepts already covered, the 64-bit network prefix plus 64-bit interface identifier split in particular.

The process begins the moment an interface comes up. First, the device generates a link-local address for itself, always in the fe80 double-colon slash 10 block, giving it something to communicate with on the local segment immediately, before it has any broader connectivity. It then performs Duplicate Address Detection, sending a neighbor solicitation message to check that no other device on the link is already using that same address; if a duplicate is found, autoconfiguration halts for that address rather than risk a conflict. Assuming no duplicate exists, the device sends a Router Solicitation message to the all-routers multicast address, ff02 double-colon 2, asking any router on the link to identify itself.

A router on the link responds with a Router Advertisement, a message that carries the network prefix in use on that link, typically a /64, along with flags indicating whether hosts should use SLAAC, use DHCPv6 instead, or use some combination of both. Routers also send these advertisements periodically and unprompted, so a device does not strictly need to solicit one; it can simply wait for the next scheduled advertisement. Once the device has the /64 prefix from the advertisement, it combines that prefix with a self-generated 64-bit interface identifier, historically derived from the interface's MAC address using a method called EUI-64, though modern operating systems more commonly generate a randomized interface identifier by default for privacy, to prevent a device from being trivially tracked across networks by a MAC-derived address that never changes.

The combination of network prefix and interface identifier produces a complete, globally valid unicast address without any central server ever allocating it or tracking its use, and the router advertisement additionally tells the host its default gateway, since the advertisement comes from that router in the first place. This is a meaningful architectural difference from IPv4, where address, gateway, and DNS server information typically all arrive together from a single DHCP transaction.

IPv6 networks can still layer DHCPv6 on top of SLAAC when centralized tracking or additional configuration options like DNS server addresses are needed, a mode often called stateless DHCPv6 when it supplies only extra options rather than the address itself, but the base address, the hardest part in IPv4's model, no longer strictly requires a server at all.
